name: Ndemli
catalog_citation: Ngoran, Loveline Lenaka. 1999. A sketch outline of the phonology of Ndemli. Maîtrise (MA) thesis, Université de Yaoundé I. vii+92 pp. (MPG PuRe item_403541, hdl:11858/00-001M-0000-0012-7FF6-E)
catalog_locator: sec. 2.3 'Ndemli tones', printed p.19 = PDF p.27 of page rendered and read as an image)
catalog_quote: Like most African languages, Ndemli is a tone language. Tone therefore plays a distinctive role, that is, a change in tone may result in a change in meaning. Tone is the relative pitch of a vocal sound. This implies that tone is contrastive because sounds are produced at different pitches. In Ndemli, pitch is also contrastive as seen in these examples: ... Ndemli is an underlyingly two-tone language, namely the high (H) and the low (L) tones. Although we find other tones like the mid (M) and contour tones at the phonetic level.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

Ndemli tones.' reads exactly 'Like most African languages, Ndemli is a tone language. Tone therefore plays a distinctive role, that is, a change in tone may result in a change in meaning. new_statements.rule_in_words: Ndemli is described as a tone language with two underlying tones (H, L) and five phonetic tones (H, M, L, falling, rising); the only accessible phonology (Ngoran 1999, and Mutaka 1994 on the same variety) says nothing at all about word stress or accent — the term never occurs. No stress placement rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: none (no stress discussion); only prosody-adjacent remark is that some vowels are reduced 'mostly towards the end of the word', chiefly after h (sec. 4.4.4, p.53-54).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical/word-level tone on noun and verb roots in citation form; phrasal H-tone spreading treated in ch.5. No word-accent domain discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Both opened sources describe the Ndemli of the Bandem area east of Yabassi (Nkam, Littoral) = ndem1249. Mutaka 1994 (JWAL 24.1) calls the language 'Yabassi' and labels it 'a dialect of Basaa (A40)'; Ngoran 1999:8 states that this paper 'tries to account for the tones of Ndemli', and Mutaka 2000 (AJAL 2:85, snippet) recounts that he was first told the language was called Yabassi — so the 1994 'Yabassi' data are Ndemli, not Basaa (basa1284).

sources.note: Nothing. The word 'stress' does not occur in the thesis (text layer grep = 0 hits; 'accent' 0 hits). Sec. 2.3 p.19 (PDF p.27): 'Like most African languages, Ndemli is a tone language... Ndemli is an underlyingly two-tone language, namely the high (H) and the low (L) tones. Although we find other tones like the mid (M) and contour tones at the phonetic level.'
